cues: The AI bubble was one man.
That's Ed Zitron's claim,
and this month,
that man resigned.
Nvidia has shed about one and a half
trillion dollars in market value in five weeks.
Anthropic cut its IPO price by nearly half.
And Zitron thinks OpenAI may never go public
at all.
This is two hours of Ed Zitron,
on Better Offline and Tech Won't Save Us,
in ten minutes.
Part one.
The man who held it together.
Zitron's argument starts years before ChatGPT.
In twenty nineteen,
Nvidia bought Mellanox,
a networking company whose technology lets thousands of
chips work as one cluster.
A year later,
Microsoft built what was then one of the
world's largest supercomputers for OpenAI,
out of Nvidia chips.
Then ChatGPT arrived,
at a moment when,
Zitron says, big tech growth had gone flat.
In his telling,
Jensen Huang sold the industry the future:
buy our chips,
do AI, and the markets will love you.
And they did.
But Zitron's math is brutal.
He estimates big tech has spent around one
point four trillion dollars,
and made maybe one hundred billion from AI.
So what kept it going?
Zitron says Jensen did,
personally.
When CoreWeave,
a former crypto miner,
needed a customer,
Nvidia agreed to rent back its own chips.
When Poolside,
an AI startup,
was running low on money,
Nvidia put in billions.
Hugging Face was bought outright.
OpenAI and Anthropic got investment promises.
In each case,
Zitron argues, the money flowed to the biggest
buyers of AI computing power.
By its last earnings,
he says,
Nvidia had over thirty billion dollars of agreements
to rent back its own chips from cloud
providers.
He compares Jensen to the Kingpin in Daredevil:
the villain who says he's the one holding
the whole city together.
And there's a reason others couldn't copy him,
he says.
Nvidia sat in what he calls free cash
flow heaven, with a spotless credit rating.
Rivals tried to sign similar deals,
but without the balance sheet,
or the nerve.
Zitron is no fan of Jensen.
But even he says:
man,
could that man sell.
Which raises the question.
If one man was holding this up,
what happened when the story about him broke?
Part two.
The story everyone ignored.
Zitron is careful about one point:
most of this was reported long before the
scandal.
In late twenty twenty-five,
the New York Times and Bloomberg reported on
Megaspeed,
a company registered in Singapore that had bought
around four point eight billion dollars of Nvidia
chips.
Bloomberg then found an almost identical company in
China, with the same website and the same
investor deck, except its data centers were in
Chinese cities.
These are reports and allegations,
and China has denied the spying claims that
came later.
But Zitron points to the short seller Culper
Research, which estimated that twenty percent or more
of Nvidia's revenue for its last fiscal year
came from China.
That's over forty-three billion dollars.
He also flags an accounting change from November
twenty twenty-five, when Nvidia began recording sales by
where a customer is headquartered rather than where
the chips are billed.
In his view,
that made it harder to see where the
chips actually went.
He describes another case from earlier this year.
A co-founder of the server maker Supermicro was
arrested and accused of trying to ship chips
to China,
allegedly using a hair dryer to peel serial
numbers off servers.
Then came the part that made it front-page
news.
Jensen Huang admitted to a relationship with Megaspeed's
chief executive, apologized to his family and his
staff, and stepped down.
Reports have also described Nvidia's general counsel contacting
the Commerce Department about its investigation.
Zitron calls the coverage one of the biggest
media failures he has seen,
because, he says,
the smuggling story sat in plain sight for
a year.
His guest on Better Offline,
Ed Elson of the Prof G Markets podcast,
raises the open question:
how much did Jensen actually know?
That,
he says, is what any investigation will turn
on.
And while Nvidia was falling,
the AI industry was about to hold its
biggest IPO ever.
Part three.
The IPO that shrank.
Anthropic, the maker of Claude,
is going public.
According to Ed Elson,
it hoped for a valuation near two trillion
dollars.
Now the range is closer to one to
one point four trillion,
and the amount it wants to raise has
dropped from about one hundred billion dollars to
sixty-five billion.
Why the discount?
Both men point to the filing itself.
Anthropic disclosed eight hundred ninety-five billion dollars of
commitments, mostly for computing power,
spread over the coming years.
Elson estimates its compute bill could jump to
one hundred to one hundred fifty billion dollars
next year.
Meanwhile, growth is slowing.
Zitron says quarterly revenue growth fell from around
one hundred fifty percent to forty-seven percent,
and data from the spending platform Ramp,
he says, points even lower for this quarter.
That brief moment when Anthropic looked profitable?
Zitron argues it came from a temporary discount
on computing power,
and that the company described in the filing
no longer really exists.
But here's the balance.
Elson actually defends Anthropic on one point.
He expected creative accounting,
the kind of numbers that strip out training
costs.
Instead, the losses are in the income statement,
and the filing openly warns that heavy spending
will change its cash flow.
On the scale of dodginess in AI,
he puts Anthropic on the less dodgy side.
Zitron's sharper worry is about who buys in.
The point of an IPO,
he says, used to be getting in early,
like Google at twenty-six billion dollars.
At over a trillion,
where is the upside for ordinary investors?
If this video is helping you make sense
of the AI money story,
subscribing is how you'll catch the next chapter.
Because the next question is whether the money
is still there.
Part four.
Is the music still playing?
Elson borrows a line from the film Margin
Call.
On Wall Street, the job is to listen to the
music, and to know when it's about to
stop.
His read:
the music is still playing.
Meta's twenty-five billion dollar stock sale was five
times oversubscribed.
An Amazon bond deal drew more than sixty
billion dollars of orders.
Microsoft pulled off one of the most sought-after
debt offerings on record.
Investors still trust companies with real cash flow.
But the notes are going out of tune.
Bond yields at CoreWeave have soared.
OpenAI cut its funding target.
And now Anthropic's IPO has shrunk.
To Elson,
it's the clearest signal yet that the music
is getting quieter.
The bigger shift,
he says,
is that big tech used to pay for
its ambitions out of its own profits.
Now it needs outside money.
He points to nearly a trillion dollars of
planned debt from the big cloud companies by
twenty twenty-eight.
Meta alone,
he notes, has a sixty billion dollar equity
raise planned for next year.
Zitron puts it in one line.
The stock market measures how excited you should
be.
The bond market measures how scared you should
be.
And he notes reports that Anthropic could get
a below investment grade rating on its debt,
which would shut out many pension and investment
funds.
And venture capital?
Asked what it measures,
Zitron's answer is not polite.
Private investors, both men agree,
were the easiest crowd of all.
Which brings us to the company that leaned
on that crowd the most.
Part five.
OpenAI, ten times worse?
Elson's view is blunt.
Whatever has gone wrong at Anthropic,
he says, it's ten times worse at OpenAI.
Anthropic lost a little over a billion dollars
on an operating basis in the first three
quarters of this year.
OpenAI,
he says, lost more than twenty billion last
year.
Then there's the fundraising.
According to Zitron,
OpenAI went to investors in the Middle East
hoping to raise thirty billion dollars at a
one point four trillion dollar valuation.
It came back with eleven billion,
at one point two five trillion.
Zitron points out that eleven billion is roughly
the size of one quarter's operating loss.
And OpenAI, he says,
has around seven hundred fifty billion dollars of
commitments through twenty thirty,
plus hundreds of millions of free users whose
chatbot use costs real money to serve.
When OpenAI talks up a billion-dollar annualized run
rate from ads,
Zitron's reply is simple:
stop using run rates.
His prediction is the boldest of the two
hours: that OpenAI may never go public at

He also cites Ramp data suggesting around eighty
percent of OpenAI and Anthropic's business revenue comes
from just one percent of customers,
mostly startups funded by venture money.
Elson expects a different path:
the era of down rounds,
when companies valued sky high in private markets
face the public market's price check.
And he has a warning for founders who
trust their backers.
Investors, he says,
are not like your parents.
They will let you die.
Zitron adds that venture capital has been on
a long losing streak,
returning roughly ninety cents to a dollar thirty
for each dollar invested since the late twenty-tens.
So with Nvidia leaderless,
Anthropic discounted and OpenAI short of cash,
what happens now?
Part six.
Without Jensen.
This is where Zitron's opening claim comes back.
In his view,
AI was always a confidence game,
and Jensen Huang was its number one salesman.
The industry, he says,
doesn't just need to stay this big.
It needs to keep growing every single year.
Without Jensen backstopping deals,
he doesn't see anyone who can do that.
He points to Elon Musk,
who he says is trying to raise forty
billion dollars to buy more Nvidia chips.
Imagine walking into a bank today,
he says,

careful and dull,

He calls this the beginning of the unraveling,

Now the balance.
Elson's view is that for the strongest companies,
the music is still playing,
and investors are still lending to businesses with
real cash flow.
Zitron himself says Nvidia is not Enron:
real things were built,
and real chips were sold.
And the cases against Nvidia's leadership are still
allegations, not verdicts.
So what should you watch?
Three things, from these two conversations.
How Anthropic's shares trade after the IPO.
Whether lenders keep funding AI debt,
and at what price.
And whether OpenAI can raise its next round.
This is their analysis,
not financial advice.
If Zitron is right,
the AI boom was never just a technology
story.
